cue: Do I parallel? (Does Tom like work parallelized — parallel tool calls, parallel agents, fan-out — and with what caveats?)
the_answer: Yes — Tom strongly favors parallelizing independent work: batch independent tool calls into one round, delegate mechanical/grunt work to agents ('tokens are for thinking'), and fan out parallel research/review agents then synthesize. The caveats are all about PROPORTIONALITY and COST: match the fan-out to the actual problem size (45 agents on a 50-line diff is overkill; 2 reviewers found the same bug), eliminate-then-batch-then-parallelize (never jump straight to parallelism), and cap/flag cost before heavy fan-outs (a deep-research run that burned a 5-hr budget / 104 agents / 2.9M tokens and died at synthesis is the cautionary tale — default research to light, 1-3 searches). Note: this is the *workflow* sense of parallel. The separate 'parallel SESSIONS on the live brain' question is more guarded (write-contention caused a recall regression; he went back to single-window for brain infra work) — adjacent, not the same thing.

essential.title: Delegate grunt work to agents — tokens are for thinking
essential.why: The clearest direct statement of the YES half of the preference, in Tom's own words ('important principle, to delegate grunt work to agents'). Establishes that parallelizing/offloading mechanical work to agents is a stated workflow rule, reserving the main thread for thinking. This is the core of 'do I parallel'.

essential.title: Tom's 'overkill' calibration: 2-reviewer pass for small surgical diffs — validated against 45-agent alternative
essential.why: The crispest statement of the CAVEAT half, grounded and empirical: Tom's 'a bit of an overkill?' on a 45-agent harness for a 50-line diff, and the validated result that a 2-reviewer pass found the same bug at a fraction of cost. Directly answers 'with what caveats' — match fan-out depth to change scope; max-effort earns its keep only on large/unfamiliar/high-stakes work.

essential.title: Rule: Optimization order — eliminate, then batch, then parallelize (locked)
essential.why: Locked rule that orders the instinct: parallelism is the THIRD lever, not the first. 'Never jump to parallelism without first asking what work can be eliminated entirely.' This is the disciplined frame around Tom's pro-parallel stance — answers the 'with what caveats' precisely (don't parallelize wasteful work).

silver.title: Proportionality check: large architectural change for small upstream gap is overreaction
silver.why: The generalized proportionality principle behind 174ad767 (which strengthens it). Same caveat at the design-decision level — size the response to the measured gap. Supports the 'don't over-fan-out' nuance even though it's not specifically about agents.

silver.title: Parallel research agents as session methodology — five deep dives synthesized in one session
silver.why: A concrete positive instance of Tom's pro-parallel methodology: launch N research agents in parallel, synthesize as results land. Shows the fan-out pattern is one Tom actively deploys (the YES half, instantiated).

silver.title: Correction: 3.5hr simulation → under 2min via pre-filter + batch + parallel
silver.why: The originating correction for the eliminate/batch/parallelize rule — concrete instance where parallelism (5-wide API calls) was the final speedup lever after eliminating and batching. Supporting evidence for the disciplined-parallelism stance.

silver.title: Test inventory 2026-05-29: 70 files, ~1,100 test functions, 8 parallel agents used
silver.why: Another concrete instance of large-surface parallel agent fan-out (8 agents) that Tom approved/used — the parallel-scan-then-single-synthesizer pattern applied to code review. Specific instance, not the principle.

silver.title: Tom stopped using the parallel session — single-window mode resumed
silver.why: Important DISAMBIGUATION / boundary: parallel SESSIONS on the live brain are a different and more guarded thing than parallel tool-calls/agents. Write-contention caused a recall regression and Tom reverted to single-window for brain infra work. Surfacing this prevents over-claiming 'Tom loves all parallelism' — it's a caveat on one specific kind.

silver.title: Parallel session decision model: observation-only from Anchor, fire-and-forget for independent work
silver.why: Nuance on WHEN parallel sessions are right: 'genuinely independent work with no coordination needs.' The independence criterion is the same one that governs parallel tool calls. Adjacent supporting nuance.

silver.title: Parallel backfill: idle-gate + worker cap pattern for safe concurrency
silver.why: Shows the cost/contention caveat in a systems context: parallelism is worth it only with an idle gate + worker cap, else it contends with live recall. Reinforces 'parallel, but capped' as a recurring Tom value.

encode_gaps.what: The specific cautionary rule: 'deep-research workflow burned a 5-hr budget (104 agents / 2.9M tokens) and died at synthesis; default research to LIGHT (1-3 WebSearch); flag cost before heavy fan-outs.'
encode_gaps.where_it_lives: MEMORY.md auto-memory file feedback_cap_heavy_token_ops.md (~/.claude/projects/-Users-tpac-brain/memory/). NOT retrievable as a brain node — multiple targeted recalls (cost-cap, 104 agents, 2.9M tokens, fan-out) failed to surface any node carrying this incident or the 'default to light' rule.
encode_gaps.impact: This is arguably the single most ANSWER-RELEVANT artifact for the cue's 'with what caveats' — it's the hardest, most quantified cost-cap on fan-out — yet it would not surface via brain recall. The brain holds the proportionality principle abstractly (174ad767, ab7bd2ef) but not this concrete fan-out-cost incident. Worth encoding as a lesson/correction node so recall can answer fully.

encode_gaps.what: The 'thoroughness, not exhaustiveness — six parallel research agents when two would answer is overcorrecting; scope to what the decision needs' framing.
encode_gaps.where_it_lives: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user global bias-override instructions, 'Compression bias' / Output Biases section). Instruction-layer, not a brain node.
encode_gaps.impact: Directly states the calibration on agent fan-out count. 174ad767 expresses the same idea empirically (45 vs 2), but the explicit 'don't over-fan-out research agents' rule lives only in instructions. Mild encode-gap — partially covered by 174ad767, so lower priority than the first gap.
